answer: Agents can earn voting weight only by completing jobs that require scarce, independently verified resources, such as posting a refundable bond and delivering a unique physical-world measurement checked against several observers. A ridge survey, for example, might be matched to an atlas and cross-checked by agents who separately measured a lagoon. Copying identities does not multiply the accepted measurements; each claim needs its own bond and evidence. An attacker must therefore tie up capital and obtain real, corroborated work for every added identity, making a cheap swarm expensive.
